1.pericope_label: The word came the second time, while he was shut up in the court of the prison
debates: What the pronoun in the second verse refers to
Whether the verbs of making are past or future
Why the promise is repeated a second time
outliers: Clarke would replace the word Lord with the divine name in all such places, and prefers the doer of it to the maker thereof
themes: Comfort delivered to a prisoner
Repetition required by distrust as much as by disobedience
A city exempted by privilege from the common lot of cities
A promise grounded on the titles of the one who makes it

3.pericope_label: Call unto me, and I will answer thee, and shew thee great and mighty things
debates: Whether the invitation to call is addressed to the prophet alone
Whether the houses were pulled down for materials or destroyed by the engines
Where the division between the fourth and fifth verses should fall
outliers: Calvin holds the verse division faulty and joins the participle of the fifth verse to the sword of the fourth
themes: A promise of answer given to a man already praying
Grief traced to slowness in asking
Houses demolished by the defenders themselves
Courage described in order to be ridiculed

6.pericope_label: I will bring it health and cure, and will reveal abundance of peace
debates: Whether the healing promised is national or spiritual
Whether the second noun means truth, peace or access to prayer
Whether the return of both kingdoms fixes the date beyond the exile
outliers: Calvin reports and rejects a rendering that would make the verse promise an access to prayer, calling it far-fetched
themes: A plaster made as large as the sore
Sickness of the body used for sickness of the state
Correction moderated before mercy is promised
Two kingdoms named where only one returned

8.pericope_label: I will cleanse them from all their iniquity, and will pardon
debates: Whether the first verb means cleansing or expiation
Why forgiveness is stated twice over
Whether the trembling of the nations is fear or awe
outliers: Calvin denies that the word for cleansing means regeneration, calling that a mistake of those unacquainted with scriptural usage
themes: Guilt enlarged in order to enlarge the pardon
Forgiveness made the basis of the promised covenant
A name that becomes a cause of joy when spoken
Nations moved by what was done rather than by what was built

10.pericope_label: The voice of joy and the voice of gladness shall be heard again
debates: Where the sentence division between the tenth and eleventh verses falls
What the streets named are
Whether the joy promised is domestic, liturgical or evangelical
outliers: Calvin hears in the description of the desolation a reproach to those who by despairing shut out the deliverance offered them
themes: A promise made concrete by naming the place
Despair treated as an obstacle to its own remedy
Marriage songs and temple songs restored together
Restoration counted the people’s honour because God gets the glory

12.pericope_label: A habitation of shepherds causing their flocks to lie down
debates: Why shepherds are chosen as the image of the restored state
Whether the promise is confined to herdsmen
What the counting of the flocks signifies
outliers: Calvin anticipates the objection that the promise would be limited to shepherds, and answers that the image stands for a general guardianship
themes: Peace measured by whether flocks dare go out
Spies looking for herdsmen as a sign of plunder
Every district of the land named in turn
Ordinary work resumed as the proof of security

14.pericope_label: Behold, the days come that I will perform that good thing which I have promised
debates: Whether the passage from this verse to the end is genuine
Whether the verb means to raise up or to establish
Why the promise is set at so long a distance
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch report four scholars who treat the rest of the chapter as spurious or interpolated, and five who defend it
themes: A section absent from the Greek and disputed on that ground
Promises described as lying dormant before they appear
Righteousness imparted rather than achieved
A priesthood widened to all who offer themselves

16.pericope_label: In those days shall Judah be saved, and this is the name wherewith she shall be called
debates: Whether the name belongs to the city or to the King
Whether the salvation promised is temporal or spiritual
Whether the pronoun is feminine or a masculine affix in the Chaldaic form
outliers: Clarke calls the received translation ignorant and almost impious and prefers the conjecture of Blayney
Wesley denies that the name is anywhere given to the church, Jewish or Christian
themes: A title transferred between a King and a city
Three covenants renewed after the captivity
A promise uttered when the line that carried it seemed to be dying out
Kingship and priesthood as the marks of a true church

18.pericope_label: Neither shall the priests the Levites want a man before me
debates: What the combination naming the priests the Levites signifies
How a promise of a perpetual Levitical priesthood is fulfilled
Whether the ceremonies named are to be taken for the realities they signified
outliers: Calvin says the priesthood had become so corrupt that the sacerdotal name itself was a profanation of sacred things
themes: A promise fulfilled otherwise than its words appeared to imply
A corrupted institution pointing beyond itself
A part named where the whole is meant
The order of nature offered as the measure of a promise

20.pericope_label: If ye can break my covenant of the day, then may my covenant with David be broken
debates: Whether the challenge carries a reproof of the people
Why the promise is narrowed from all the tribes to two families
What the multiplied seed of David refers to
outliers: Clarke argues from the extinction of both priestly families that the priesthood promised here can only be a spiritual one
themes: The order of nature made the measure of a covenant
Complaint treated as an attempt to unmake the world
A part named for the whole
Rulers and priests held to exist for the people and not for themselves

23.pericope_label: The two families which the LORD hath chosen, these he hath rejected
debates: Which two families the people meant
Whether the scornful saying came from the Chaldeans or from the Jews themselves
Whether Jacob stands in the place of Aaron at the last verse
outliers: Clarke rejects both the two kingdoms and the families of Jacob and David as not being distinct families at all
Gill reports and rejects a rabbinic reading that puts Jacob in the place of Aaron
themes: A saying of despair answered rather than rebuked
Repetition defended as necessary against hopelessness
The order of nature offered a second time as the measure of a promise
Patience required until an appointed term
